There is an obvious difference between al-Shahrastānī’s account and the accounts given by al-Ashʿarī and al-Khayyāṭ.
Al-Shahrastānī seems to say that it is the accidents that are infinite in Maʿmar’s theory. The other two texts say that the meanings themselves are infinite.
But the difference is not fundamental.
If every accident requires a “meaning” behind it, as Maʿmar argues, then an infinite series of accidents also requires an infinite series of meanings.

What the theory seems to imply, then, is that every event in our material world belongs to an endless chain of “meanings.” These meanings are connected with one another, yet each remains distinct, and the whole chain exists at the same time.
Take the movement of a body. That movement depends on an immediate meaning that acts as its cause. Without it, the movement would not happen and the body would not move.

But this meaning itself depends on another meaning that makes it active and gives it the power to produce movement. The second meaning then depends on a third, which plays the same role in relation to it, and so on without end.
Are they simple spiritual substances connected with Plato’s world of Forms, or with the separate intellects of Plotinus?
Are they generative causes, each producing the next in a chain like Aristotle’s series of causes or movers?
Or are they simply a chain of secondary causes?
The texts we have about Maʿmar al-Sulamī and the Maʿmariyya do not give us a clear answer.
The modern scholar Dr ʿAlī Sāmī al-Nashshār, whose own outlook is Ashʿarite, draws attention to another statement attributed to Maʿmar himself:
Al-Nashshār then tries to connect this statement about God’s attributes with Maʿmar’s “meanings” in the natural world. From this connection, he develops a metaphysical interpretation of the theory.

He writes, in effect, that these meanings must be the divine attributes. The meanings are simple because God’s attributes are simple. The meanings are infinite in number, and God’s attributes are infinite in number. The series of meanings has no end, and God’s attributes have no end. Finally, these meanings are mental considerations, because an attribute is itself a mental way of considering the divine essence.

Al-Nashshār concludes that Maʿmar solved the problem of the divine attributes through this extremely subtle and difficult theory. He rejects the other interpretations given by historians of Muʿtazilite thought.
In our view, however, Maʿmar’s theory of “meanings” is a philosophical explanation of the natural world.
Despite the confusion in the texts, their internal logic seems much closer to Aristotle’s explanation of movement in nature and to his chain of movers ending in the eternal First Mover.

Al-Nashshār’s attempt to connect the “meanings” that Maʿmar uses to explain movement in nature with the “meanings” mentioned in the statement about God’s attributes requires a long chain of comparisons.

Those comparisons begin mainly from the fact that the same word, “meanings,” appears in both places. Al-Nashshār also assumes that the meanings behind natural movement are simple. He then builds further comparisons on that assumption until he reaches the conclusion that Maʿmar’s “meanings” in the material world are really the divine attributes.
But this assumption needs convincing evidence from the texts themselves.
The Maʿmariyya also held a distinctive view of the description of God as qadīm, meaning eternal or without beginning.
Al-Shahrastānī and al-Baghdādī both say that Maʿmar denied that God should be called qadīm. Al-Baghdādī adds that Maʿmar still described God as “existing eternally.”

Al-Shahrastānī explains Maʿmar’s reasoning through the Arabic word itself. Qadīm comes from a verb connected with something having existed earlier or having become old. On this reading, the word carries a suggestion of time.
But God’s existence is not temporal.

Maʿmar’s reasoning here therefore rests on the linguistic logic of the word qadīm and on the way it is derived from a verb. If the description comes from an action, and action is tied to time, then describing God as qadīm would suggest existence through time. Yet God’s existence is not in time.
Al-Ashʿarī, however, reports another statement by Maʿmar:
“I do not say that the Creator is qadīm except once He has brought created things into existence.”
This suggests that for Maʿmar the description qadīm is relative rather than absolute.
God is called qadīm only in relation to created things that come into existence after Him.
In our view, this is the correct way to understand Maʿmar’s position.
This question of God’s eternity, and the attempt to study it through the temporal logic built into the word itself, later became a major subject in the work of Muslim theologians and philosophers.
Here again, we can see the Muʿtazilites laying the foundations for later discussions.
Maʿmar and his followers also held a distinctive view of God’s attribute of knowledge.

“Jaʿfar ibn Ḥarb reported that Maʿmar said: it is impossible for God to know Himself, because that would mean that the knower and the known were not one and the same. And it is impossible for Him to know anything other than Himself, just as it is said that it is impossible for Him to exercise power over something that already exists simply insofar as it exists.”

“Because this man inclined toward the philosophers, and because their doctrine holds that the Creator does not possess receptive knowledge—that is, knowledge that follows and is affected by the thing known—but rather active knowledge, He knows insofar as He acts. His knowledge is what brings the act about. It therefore relates to a thing when that thing comes into existence, but cannot relate to something that remains nonexistent.”
According to al-Shahrastānī’s account, then, Maʿmar believed that God cannot know either Himself or something other than Himself.
Why can God not know Himself?

Because if God knows Himself, then within the divine essence there would have to be both a knower and something known. Knowledge normally involves two sides: the one who knows and the thing that is known.
That would introduce multiplicity into God.
For Maʿmar, this would violate the first of the Muʿtazilites’ five main principles: divine unity.
Why, then, can God not know something other than Himself?
Because knowing something normally means being affected by that thing. The thing known acts on the knower in some way.
But the philosophers held that God’s knowledge is not passive or receptive. It does not depend on something outside God and is not affected by it.
In other words, it does not receive its object; it produces it.
God’s knowledge is itself what brings the act into existence.

For this reason, Maʿmar can still describe God as “knowing” a particular thing once that thing comes into existence. But he cannot say that God knows it before it exists. Before then it is nonexistent, and how could God know something while it remains nonexistent if His knowledge is itself an act—that is, an act of bringing something into existence?

We can see philosophical thinking gradually becoming more visible here and entering every area of Muʿtazilite thought, even while the Muʿtazilites continued to work within the framework of one or another of their five main religious principles.
B — The Question of the Created Qurʾān
We said earlier that the Muʿtazilite understanding of divine unity led them to adopt a number of rational positions that differed sharply from those of the traditionalists.
One of these concerned God’s attributes, which we have already discussed at length. But that discussion is not yet finished.
The question of the created Qurʾān is one of its most important branches.
This question produced some of the fiercest and, at times, bloodiest conflicts in the history of Arab-Islamic thought. Those conflicts reached deeply into social and political life.
Yet despite these dangerous consequences, the issue retained a degree of relative independence at the intellectual level. This allowed it to develop into a much deeper theoretical problem.

In doing so, it helped push Arab-Islamic thought further toward the philosophical and scientific forms it was beginning to seek. These first took shape in kalām, or systematic theology, and later reached their fullest form in what we call Arab-Islamic philosophy.
So where did the question come from, and what was it really about?
Its origin lies in the Muʿtazilite debate over God’s attributes.

Once the Muʿtazilites had declared that God’s essence and attributes were one, and had therefore denied the existence of attributes added to the essence, they had to deal with the attributes mentioned in religious texts.
Their method was to interpret these texts rationally in a way that agreed with their understanding of divine unity.
Among the attributes mentioned in the texts, they found speech.
The Qurʾān itself is also described as “the speech of God,” as in the verse:
“If any of the polytheists asks you for protection, grant him protection so that he may hear the speech of God.”
Here, “the speech of God” means the Qurʾān itself.
God is therefore described as one who speaks, and the Qurʾān is described as His speech.
What were the Muʿtazilites to do with this attribute?
Could they say that speech was one of the attributes identical with the divine essence?
If they did, they would have to say that this attribute was permanent and unchanging, because in their system there was an absolute identity between God’s essence and His attributes.
They all agreed that God’s essence cannot change. The attributes would therefore have to be equally unchanging.
But if God’s speech is fixed and unchanging, a problem immediately appears in the Qurʾān itself.
The Qurʾān contains many different kinds of speech. There are commands and prohibitions, promises and threats, laws, reports and descriptions.

If the attribute of “speaking” is identical with God’s essence, and if the Qurʾān is God’s speech, then the variety and difference within this speech would imply variety and difference within the divine essence itself.

The final result would be a denial of the unity of the divine essence. This would contradict the Muʿtazilite principle of divine unity—and indeed the principle of divine unity accepted by Muslims in general.
The Muʿtazilites therefore argued that God’s speech is not qadīm—not eternal and identical with the divine essence.
It is something that came into existence.
The Qurʾān, which all of them accepted as God’s speech, therefore came into existence as well.
In other words, it is created, just like everything else in the created universe.
To say that God “speaks,” on this view, simply means that God creates speech.
This is the origin and basic meaning of the question as the Muʿtazilites understood it.
But they did not stop there.

They also tried to support their position with other arguments. Some of these aimed to show that belief in an eternal Qurʾān did not merely conflict with divine unity. It also conflicted with the rational character of Qurʾānic law.
Suppose the Qurʾān were eternal speech—that is, an eternal attribute of the eternal divine essence.
Then the commands contained in the Qurʾān would also have to be eternal.
But that would mean that God’s commands existed before the people to whom they were addressed existed.
Before human beings existed, there would have been no one for the commands to apply to.
Human beings are the subjects of these commands.
How, then, could God issue commands to people who did not yet exist?
The Muʿtazilites argued that this would be meaningless, and meaningless action cannot be attributed to God.
They also said that speech requires both someone who speaks and someone who is addressed.
Before the people subject to God’s commands existed, there would have been a speaker but no listener or addressee.
For this reason, they argued, belief in an eternal Qurʾān would make divine legislation irrational, and the claim must therefore be false.
